what_it_does: At the sub-3-nanometer scale that TSMC's most advanced chip manufacturing uses, the rules for how transistors can be arranged become extremely restrictive. FinFlex is a technique that allows cells (the small standard building blocks from which chips are assembled) to come in multiple heights and with different threshold voltages — the voltage at which a transistor turns on — trading off between speed, power, and area. Legalization is the step in chip design where cells that were placed approximately are snapped to legal positions on the manufacturing grid. This paper tackles legalization under an additional constraint called minimum implant area (MIA): regions of the chip where a certain material is implanted must meet a minimum size, or the manufacturing process fails. The proposed three-stage approach first preprocesses cells to fix obvious violations while respecting timing and power goals, then uses a directed acyclic graph (a network with no cycles, used to represent ordering constraints) for an initial legal placement with cell-version substitution, and finally applies dynamic programming (a method that solves a problem by combining solutions to smaller sub-problems) to clean up remaining MIA violations across rows.
